dimensions.name: Fairness Evaluation — Fair & Representative Training Data Assurance
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for defects that make fairness evaluation of educational software incomplete, inconsistent, or misleading. Focus on the representativeness of data used for training, validation, benchmarking, evaluation, or audit; the definition and handling of fairness groups; and whether group-level evaluation can detect failures hidden by aggregate results.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Review any behavior-affecting source, test, schema, configuration, migration, query, prompt/template, data/model artifact, build/deployment file, or UI asset that is relevant to this dimension. Determine intended behavior from repository evidence before judging it. Trace relevant control and data flow through callers, callees, shared utilities, persistence, asynchronous work, and framework/library defaults as needed; do not restrict analysis to the changed lines when surrounding context is necessary. Apply every criterion below to every relevant path, and continue the review after finding an issue rather than stopping at the first plausible bug. The listed evidence signals are examples, not an exhaustive checklist. If a criterion is not applicable to the target, do not force a finding.
</review_standard>
<reporting_bar>
Report every concrete code-level defect or behaviorally meaningful defect you can ground in a reachable input, state, data flow, or execution sequence, including low-severity or uncertain issues; state uncertainty rather than silently dropping a plausible bug. For a diff/change review, a valid finding must be introduced, exposed, or materially worsened by the target; unchanged code may be used as evidence. For a file or codebase review, a valid finding must exist within the requested scope. A finding should explain the trigger and the incorrect or misleading outcome. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Unrepresentative Dataset Coverage
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether data used to train, validate, benchmark, evaluate, or audit learner-affecting behavior fails to cover the intended learner population, educational settings, sources, or case types well enough for the resulting evaluation to support the repository's stated claims.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect relevant manifests, queries, schemas, source selection, sampling, filtering, deduplication, splits, subgroup labels, coverage summaries, fixtures, benchmark composition, weighting, and aggregation. Look for intended groups or settings that are absent or severely underrepresented, selection logic that unintentionally removes them, leakage or duplication that distorts apparent coverage, or aggregate results that hide known subgroup gaps.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish the intended population and evaluation purpose from repository code, configuration, tests, schemas, documentation, or product contracts. Trace how records enter and leave the evaluated dataset and check whether stratification, weighting, balancing, coverage assertions, or separate group-level evaluation already handles the apparent gap. A valid finding requires a concrete coverage blind spot that can make an evaluation or claim misleading; dataset size alone is not evidence, and the review should not require collection of attributes the product intentionally cannot or should not collect.
</verification>

criteria.name: Undefined Fairness Evaluation Attributes
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether attributes or categories used for fairness evaluation are defined and handled consistently enough for reliable subgroup analysis.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect schemas, enums, category mappings, normalization, aliases, localization, null/unknown handling, joins, derived group fields, filtering, serialization, aggregation, and fallback paths. Look for ambiguous category meaning, inconsistent producer/consumer mappings, records silently dropped from subgroup analysis, distinct groups unintentionally collapsed, or the same value interpreted differently at different stages.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace each relevant attribute from its source through transformation to the fairness metric or report. Confirm whether a shared schema, normalization layer, or library already enforces the intended semantics. A valid finding requires a concrete way that ambiguity or inconsistent handling can change subgroup membership, metrics, or the repository's stated fairness evaluation. When group data is intentionally unavailable, evaluate the implemented fallback rather than inventing a requirement to collect more sensitive attributes.
</verification>

criteria.name: Missing Group-Wise Fairness Targets
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether an evaluation or release check can pass on aggregate performance while a defined learner subgroup violates the fairness target that the repository intends to enforce.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect metric computation, subgroup aggregation, thresholds, tolerances, assertions, acceptance gates, generated reports, configuration, CI/release checks, and tests. Look for subgroup metrics that are calculated but ignored, pass/fail logic that reads only aggregate values, incorrect group-to-threshold mappings, missing groups caused by default/fallback behavior, or tests that allow a known subgroup failure to pass validation.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish which groups and targets actually apply from repository evidence, then follow a failing subgroup value through the validation path to determine whether the overall evaluation can still succeed. Check shared evaluators and configuration before concluding a check is absent. A valid finding requires a defined fairness expectation that can be bypassed or masked; do not invent numerical thresholds or require identical outcomes across groups unless the product specifies that policy.
</verification>

criteria.name: Fairness Evaluation Pipeline Integrity
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the fairness evaluation pipeline can silently compute, cache, select, or report the wrong result even when its dataset and intended targets are otherwise valid. Preserve the fairness-evaluation focus: this criterion covers correctness defects that can change or conceal subgroup evidence, not unrelated application bugs.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace evaluation entry points through data loading, preprocessing, joins, feature and label construction, model/version selection, metric computation, aggregation, serialization, caching, report generation, and release gates. Inspect units, denominators, empty-group behavior, divide-by-zero and NaN handling, rounding, sign/direction, stale cache keys, split leakage, duplicate records, pagination, asynchronous completion, exception fallbacks, command and test execution, and producer/consumer schemas. Look for a requested cohort evaluated with another cohort's data, metrics attached to the wrong group, failures converted to zero or omitted output, partial evaluation presented as complete, or a report/check reading stale or differently configured results.
</inspect>
<verification>
Follow a concrete record or controlled metric value end to end and compare the computed and surfaced result with the repository's formulas, fixtures, schemas, configuration, or tests. Check whether another layer rejects incomplete or invalid output. A valid finding requires a reachable defect that changes, drops, mislabels, or falsely validates fairness evidence. A broken test or build is a finding here only when it prevents the configured fairness evaluation or its enforcement from executing; report general execution failures under system-integrity.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Pedagogy — Adaptive Fairness & Transparent Learner Progression Integrity
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for defects that can produce educationally inappropriate learner progression or intervention behavior. Focus on early-warning logic, persistent adverse learner state, hidden progression requirements, and adaptive sequencing or recommendations that can violate explicit pedagogical or learner-state constraints.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. For a file or codebase review, a valid finding must exist within the requested scope. A finding should explain the trigger and the incorrect or misleading outcome. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Unvalidated Early-Warning Thresholds
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether early-warning predictions, risk flags, alerts, or interventions can trigger from thresholds, confidence rules, minimum-evidence rules, timing windows, or missing-data defaults that are inconsistent with the validation or operating assumptions encoded by the product.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect threshold constants and configuration, feature windows, eligibility rules, minimum-observation checks, confidence/calibration gates, default values, missing-data behavior, model/version metadata, cohort rules, and tests. Look for off-by-one or unit errors, thresholds applied to the wrong score/version, alerts emitted before enough evidence exists, stale configuration, missing values that systematically push learners across a threshold, or a fallback path that bypasses the normal gate.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a concrete learner state from available evidence through eligibility, scoring, threshold comparison, and resulting action. Verify whether shared configuration, metadata, or downstream logic supplies the apparent guard. A valid finding requires a reachable case where the system acts outside its defined evidence/timing assumptions or uses a threshold differently from its contract. Absence of external research or validation artifacts is not itself a code defect unless the repository explicitly depends on them.
</verification>

criteria.name: Persistent Negative State
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether adverse learner state such as a risk flag, penalty, low-confidence classification, restriction, or negative score can persist or compound after the evidence that created it is stale, corrected, superseded, or no longer sufficient.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect persisted fields, caches, session restoration, event replay, cumulative formulas, recursive scoring, status transitions, expiry/decay/reset rules, recomputation triggers, retries, idempotency, manual corrections, and multi-session tests. Look for stale values reused as fresh input, transitions with no recovery path, duplicate events that compound a penalty, corrected source data that does not invalidate derived state, or an old flag that becomes evidence for a new flag.
</inspect>
<verification>
Follow at least one realistic sequence across multiple updates or sessions and determine whether fresh evidence can clear, reduce, or recompute the adverse state as intended. Check lifecycle hooks and shared state services before reporting. A valid finding requires stale or duplicated adverse state to change later learner treatment without a current valid basis. Persistence that is explicitly required, bounded, and correctly refreshed by the domain rules is not a defect.
</verification>

criteria.name: Hidden Learning Path Requirements
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a learner can be blocked, marked incomplete, redirected, or prevented from progressing by a prerequisite, completion rule, lock, deadline, eligibility condition, or required next action that the product fails to communicate accurately at the point of impact.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect progression calculations, state machines, route or navigation guards, eligibility checks, feature/configuration gates, API errors, UI locked/incomplete states, progress indicators, localization strings, and tests. Look for backend-only requirements with no surfaced reason, UI/backend disagreement about prerequisites, progress displays that omit a required step, generic errors that hide the actionable condition, or stale client state that shows a path as available when it will be rejected.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace the same blocking condition through enforcement and the final learner-visible state. Verify whether a shared component or another guaranteed layer supplies the reason and next action. A valid finding requires a reachable state where the system's communicated path conflicts with the enforced path or leaves the learner unable to determine how to proceed. Purely internal conditions that never create a learner-visible inconsistency are outside this criterion.
</verification>

criteria.name: Pedagogically Unconstrained Adaptation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether adaptive sequencing, recommendation, routing, tutoring, or intervention logic can choose an educationally invalid action because explicit pedagogical or learner-state constraints represented by the product are not enforced.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect recommenders, rankers, rules, prompts, score combination, prerequisite graphs, mastery/level state, completion state, course configuration, availability rules, fallback behavior, re-evaluation, overrides, and tests. Look for optimization scores overriding hard prerequisites, stale learner state, invalid or already-completed content being recommended, no valid fallback when top-ranked content is ineligible, or a decision that fails to update after learner state changes.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a concrete learner state through the adaptive decision and compare the selected action with explicit constraints in code, configuration, content metadata, or tests. Verify whether another guaranteed layer filters invalid results. A valid finding requires an implemented product constraint to be bypassed, misapplied, or evaluated with stale/incorrect state. The review should not invent pedagogical rules that the repository does not represent.
</verification>

criteria.name: Instructional Content Integrity and Availability
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether educational content, assessments, feedback, learner work, or progress evidence can be lost, corrupted, associated with the wrong owner or version, duplicated, truncated, or made unavailable in a way that breaks the intended teaching or learning flow.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect upload and import paths, storage keys, overwrite behavior, database/file transaction ordering, replacement and deletion callbacks, content parsing, encoding, versioning, draft/publish transitions, generated-content status, background jobs, retries, cancellation, pagination, cache invalidation, download/access paths, and cleanup. Trace both successful and failing operations. Look for a new file deleted by cleanup that targets the same key, a database row committed before its resource exists, old content served after replacement, partial generation exposed as complete, a failed import that leaves misleading progress, or a retry that duplicates questions, submissions, or feedback.
</inspect>
<verification>
Follow a concrete content artifact across create, read, update/replace, delete, failure, and retry states as applicable. Compare database identity and lifecycle with external storage or asynchronous work, and verify what learners and educators can actually retrieve. A valid finding requires a reachable loss, corruption, misassociation, duplication, stale presentation, or unavailable required artifact that materially changes an educational flow. Pure infrastructure defects with no educational-content or learner-progress consequence belong under system-integrity.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Decision Fairness — Protected Attribute Governance & Validated Fairness Enforcement
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for learner-affecting decision logic that can create unjustified differential treatment through protected attributes or proxies, rely on an unverified fairness mitigation, or fail to enforce the repository's intended separation between restricted fairness attributes and ordinary decision inputs.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Review any behavior-affecting source, test, schema, configuration, migration, query, prompt/template, data/model artifact, build/deployment file, or UI asset that is relevant to this dimension. </review_standard>

Report every concrete code-level defect or behaviorally meaningful defect you can ground in a reachable input, state, data flow, or execution sequence, including low-severity or uncertain issues; state uncertainty rather than silently dropping a plausible bug. For a diff/change review, a valid finding must be introduced, exposed, or materially worsened by the target; unchanged code may be used as evidence. For a file or codebase review, a valid finding must exist within the requested scope. A finding should explain the trigger and the incorrect or misleading outcome. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Protected and Proxy-Based Differential Treatment
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a protected attribute or a field acting as a close proxy can unjustifiably change ranking, scoring, routing, gating, recommendation, access, support, or another consequential learner outcome for otherwise comparable cases.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace relevant fields through schemas, feature construction, prompts, rules, filters, thresholds, weights, ranking, model inputs, routing, and final actions. Potential proxies can include geography, language, institution, location-derived values, coded labels, or other fields whose use is functionally tied to a protected characteristic in this product. Look for group-specific thresholds, hidden branching, accidental feature inclusion, fallback differences, or proxy values that alter the outcome without the intended policy path.
</inspect>
<verification>
Demonstrate a concrete path from the attribute or proxy to the consequential decision and compare materially similar inputs where that value differs. Establish whether the use is an intended accommodation, fairness correction, legal/product requirement, or other explicitly justified and enforced path. A valid finding requires the field to change treatment without a supported justification; field presence, correlation, or collection for measurement alone is not sufficient.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unvalidated Fairness Mitigations
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a fairness mitigation implemented in code or configuration can fail to address the disparity it is intended to reduce, or can introduce a new regression, because its effect is not validated by the evidence the repository relies on.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect group-specific thresholds, weighting, sampling, re-ranking, post-processing, routing exceptions, normalization, constraints, feature changes, associated metrics, fixtures, regression tests, and evaluation configuration. Look for a mitigation wired to the wrong group or metric, direction/sign errors, stale thresholds, code paths that bypass the mitigation, tests that only prove execution rather than effect, or available subgroup results that contradict the mitigation's intended behavior.
</inspect>
<verification>
First establish the mitigation's intended target from code, configuration, tests, documentation, or supplied review context. Trace how it affects the relevant decision or metric and compare against available before/after or expected subgroup behavior. A valid finding requires a concrete mismatch between the mitigation's intended effect and its implemented or tested behavior. Do not require a particular mitigation technique or external study when another repository-supported validation path exists.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unenforced Protected-Attribute Separation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether attributes that the repository intends to restrict to fairness evaluation, auditing, or another specially authorized purpose are actually prevented from flowing into ordinary learner decision inputs, while remaining available only where their allowed purpose requires them.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect data models, DTOs, feature builders, prompt/model inputs, queries, pipelines, storage, serializers, allowlists/denylists, permissions, service boundaries, logging, and tests. Look for an evaluation-only field accidentally copied into a general feature object, unrestricted shared records used by both decisioning and auditing, permissions that do not match the intended separation, or refactors that bypass an existing filtering boundary.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish the intended restriction from repository evidence and trace each relevant field to its actual consumers. Verify separation enforced by executable boundaries such as types, feature allowlists, access controls, serializers, or service interfaces rather than documentation alone. A valid finding requires an intended restriction to be bypassable or broken. Do not assume every protected attribute must be excluded from every decision, and do not require retention of sensitive data where the product intentionally does not collect it.
</verification>

criteria.name: Decision Policy and Outcome Integrity
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether learner-affecting eligibility, scoring, ranking, routing, access, moderation, or intervention logic can apply the wrong policy or outcome because its inputs, ownership scope, state transitions, ordering, or persistence are incorrect. Preserve the decision-fairness focus by prioritizing failures that produce inconsistent treatment between comparable learners or groups.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace request identity, tenant/course/cohort scope, normalized inputs, defaults, rule and model versions, thresholds, tie-breaking, sorting, pagination, status transitions, cache keys, database queries, transactions, retries, asynchronous jobs, and final actions. Look for one learner's state used for another, missing ownership filters, nondeterministic ties that systematically change access, stale decisions after source changes, partial writes that leave enforcement inconsistent, fallback rules that differ from primary rules, and alternate endpoints or jobs that bypass the canonical policy.
</inspect>
<verification>
Compare materially equivalent cases through every relevant decision path and follow the chosen outcome through persistence and consumption. Establish the intended policy from executable repository evidence and check centralized enforcement before reporting. A valid finding requires a reachable correctness defect that causes inconsistent or incorrect consequential treatment; a generic business-logic bug with no learner-affecting decision consequence belongs under system-integrity.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Inclusion — Cultural & Accessibility Equity in Design and Code
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for behavior that can unnecessarily exclude or disadvantage valid users of educational software through culturally narrow data assumptions, exclusionary product language, accessibility defects, or unsupported assumptions about devices, bandwidth, input methods, or location.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. For a file or codebase review, a valid finding must exist within the requested scope. A finding should explain the trigger and the incorrect or misleading outcome. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Culturally Narrow Representations and Validation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether representation, parsing, validation, storage, or formatting logic rejects, corrupts, collapses, or misinterprets valid user data from cultural or locale contexts that the educational product claims to support.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect regexes, character restrictions, field lengths, enums, normalization, Unicode handling, case conversion, locale selection, name/identity fields, date/time/number/currency/address parsing, language tags, serialization, database constraints, and tests. Look for ASCII-only assumptions, fixed locale formats, lossy normalization, incorrect timezone/locale defaults, rigid identity options where the product supports broader values, or frontend/backend validation disagreement.
</inspect>
<verification>
Produce a concrete valid input or supported locale that is rejected, corrupted, mis-stored, or mapped incorrectly, and trace it through all relevant layers. Check internationalization libraries and downstream normalization before reporting. A valid finding requires a mismatch with the product's supported domain; support for arbitrary worldwide formats is not required when the product explicitly has a narrower scope.
</verification>

criteria.name: Exclusionary Language in Code and UI
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether behaviorally meaningful or user-facing language in the target stigmatizes, excludes, or misrepresents supported users, or encodes an assumption that causes the product to communicate or behave incorrectly toward them.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect learner-, educator-, and administrator-facing strings, errors, labels, generated text templates, prompts, exported reports, canonical categories, and identifiers or comments only when they feed generated behavior, public/developer contracts, or product semantics. Look for unnecessarily gendered defaults, one group labeled as the normal/default and others as deviations, deprecated discriminatory terminology, hostile wording, or language/category mappings that lead to incorrect user-visible classification.
</inspect>
<verification>
Evaluate the wording in its actual audience and domain context and trace whether it reaches product behavior or an externally meaningful contract. Check for required quotations, third-party protocol terms, historical fixtures, and neutral technical terminology. A valid finding requires a concrete exclusionary or misleading effect in a supported context; purely private naming/style preferences with no behavioral or user-facing consequence are not findings.
</verification>

criteria.name: Excluding Access Assumptions
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a supported learner or educator flow becomes unusable, inaccessible, or materially degraded because the implementation assumes a particular input method, sensory ability, viewport/device capability, bandwidth level, or location without an equivalent supported path.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect semantic HTML/component roles, accessible names, labels, form associations, focus order, keyboard operation, pointer-only interactions, ARIA, status/error announcements, color-only meaning, contrast tokens, media alternatives, responsive behavior, zoom/reflow, asset loading, network/offline fallbacks, device capability checks, geolocation gates, and tests. Use the repository's declared accessibility standard when one exists; otherwise evaluate concrete platform semantics and supported user flows rather than inventing a compliance target.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a specific supported flow using the affected input method, assistive behavior, device state, network state, or location condition. Verify browser/framework/component-library defaults and shared wrappers before attributing the failure to the target. A valid finding requires a reachable barrier or materially incorrect behavior, such as an unlabeled interactive control, keyboard trap, inaccessible status change, broken supported viewport, or mandatory capability with no supported alternative.
</verification>

criteria.name: Misleading or Unrecoverable Supported Flows
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a supported user is falsely told that data is empty, work succeeded, access is unavailable, or no next action exists when the real state is loading, partial, stale, unauthorized, rate-limited, offline, or failed. Focus on whether ordinary failure and boundary conditions exclude users from completing or recovering a supported flow.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace API and server failures, rejected promises, timeouts, cancellation, loading and empty states, retry and resume controls, form validation, upload limits and accepted types, disabled controls, optimistic updates, partial pagination, session expiry, feature availability, localization, and assistive announcements. Compare documented hints and UI constraints with backend validators and infrastructure limits. Look for non-success responses converted to empty arrays or null success values, perpetual loading, errors swallowed without a retry path, contradictory size/type guidance, rejected work that remains displayed as saved, or recovery controls unavailable by keyboard or screen reader.
</inspect>
<verification>
Drive a concrete supported flow through at least one boundary or failure state and trace the exact state delivered to the user. Check shared error boundaries, data libraries, retries, and guaranteed global notifications before reporting. A valid finding requires a user-visible false state, blocked recovery, silent loss of submitted work, or materially incorrect constraint that prevents supported use. A backend failure that is accurately surfaced and recoverable is not a finding merely because failure is possible.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Transparency — Transparent, Explainable, Validated & Human-Supervised AI Decisioning
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for AI, statistical, analytics, or algorithmic behavior that users can materially misinterpret or cannot meaningfully supervise. Focus on opaque decision outputs, causal overclaiming, prediction use outside validated scope, one-way consequential decisions, and automation that bypasses safeguards required by the product.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Review any behavior-affecting source, test, schema, configuration, migration, query, prompt/template, data/model artifact, build/deployment file, or UI asset that is relevant to this dimension. Report every concrete code-level defect or behaviorally meaningful defect you can ground in a reachable input, state, data flow, or execution sequence, including low-severity or uncertain issues; state uncertainty rather than silently dropping a plausible bug. For a diff/change review, a valid finding must be introduced, exposed, or materially worsened by the target; unchanged code may be used as evidence. For a file or codebase review, a valid finding must exist within the requested scope. A finding should explain the trigger and the incorrect or misleading outcome. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Opaque AI Decision Outputs
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a learner-, educator-, or administrator-facing AI or algorithmic score, label, placement, flag, recommendation, or action is presented in a way that can materially mislead the user about what it means, why it is being used, or how certain/limited it is under the product's own transparency requirements.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace the output through model/rule execution, response schemas, transformations, generated summaries, UI rendering, explanation fields, confidence/uncertainty metadata, status labels, audit fields, and tests. Look for meaning lost between backend and UI, confidence shown as certainty, an explanation attached to the wrong decision, raw internal values exposed without required interpretation, or limitations/explanations dropped on one path but present on another.
</inspect>
<verification>
Evaluate the final consumed output, not an isolated lower-level return value, and verify whether a guaranteed downstream layer supplies the required context. Establish the transparency expectation from repository/product evidence or from the consequence level encoded by the workflow. A valid finding requires a concrete path where the surfaced output can be materially misread because required meaning, provenance, uncertainty, or limitation information is missing or incorrect. Never require disclosure of chain-of-thought, sensitive internals, or proprietary model details.
</verification>

criteria.name: Causal Overclaiming in Analytics
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product presents observational, correlational, predictive, or descriptive analytics as a causal explanation of learner outcomes when the underlying implementation does not support that claim.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect metric definitions, statistical calculations, chart titles, labels, tooltips, annotations, reports, generated summaries, prompt/templates that produce analytics copy, API fields whose names surface to users, and tests. Look for correlation or feature importance rendered as cause, risk scores explained as reasons, certainty language introduced after a transformation, or a disclaimer present in one channel but omitted in another.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace the surfaced claim back to the computation and determine what kind of inference the implementation actually supports. Check whether the repository contains an experimental, causal, or otherwise valid design justifying the language. A valid finding requires a user- or decision-facing causal claim that is stronger than the underlying evidence. Internal variable names alone are not findings unless they drive surfaced language or behavior.
</verification>

criteria.name: Mismatched Prediction Validation and Use
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a prediction, risk score, classifier, or similar validated decision component is used for a population, outcome, timing window, feature definition, threshold, or decision purpose that differs materially from the scope represented by its repository validation or configuration.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect model and configuration metadata, feature pipelines, population/cohort filters, label definitions, versions, serving routes, thresholds, call sites, UI actions, fallbacks, and tests. Look for version/config skew, a model reused by a new caller with different semantics, changed label meaning, out-of-scope population routing, thresholds copied from another use case, or preprocessing differences between evaluation and serving.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish both the validated/declared scope and the actual use from code, configuration, tests, or supplied model documentation, then trace a concrete request across the mismatch. A valid finding requires the implementation to permit materially different use without a corresponding supported validation/configuration path. If the validated scope cannot be established from available evidence, state that limitation rather than guessing it.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unidirectional Algorithmic Decisions Without Educator Contestability
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a consequential algorithmic decision can affect a learner while the authorized human actors defined by the product have no effective way to provide correcting context, contest an incorrect result, request review, or have an accepted correction influence the decision state.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect feedback/appeal flows, override APIs, reviewer queues, permissions, human-context fields, persistence, audit logs, event routing, recomputation, state transitions, UI states, and tests. Look for controls that exist only visually, feedback that is stored but never consumed, an override that is later overwritten by recomputation, missing authorization on correction paths, or a review request that cannot change the consequential state.
</inspect>
<verification>
First establish that the output is consequential and that the product provides or requires contestability for the relevant actor. Trace a concrete correction or appeal from submission through persistence to downstream behavior and check alternate review paths. A valid finding requires the implemented contestability path to be absent when required, unreachable, ineffective, or inconsistent. Purely informational outputs do not require a contestability mechanism unless the repository says otherwise.
</verification>

criteria.name: Automation Without Review Safeguards
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a consequential learner-affecting action can execute automatically while bypassing an approval, permission, override, reversal, or other human-review safeguard that the product requires for that action.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect handlers, jobs, queues, workflows/state machines, role and permission checks, approval states, feature flags, retries, race conditions, scheduled actions, rollback/reversal paths, audit logs, and tests. Look for execution before approval commits, stale approval reused after inputs change, alternate endpoints/jobs that bypass the gate, unauthorized actors able to approve/override, retry paths that duplicate a consequential action, or reversal that does not restore dependent state.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish the action's consequence and the applicable safeguard from repository/product evidence, then trace a concrete path to execution. Check upstream and downstream enforcement as well as concurrency/retry behavior before reporting. A valid finding requires an applicable safeguard to be bypassed, incorrectly enforced, or ineffective. Low-impact automation that the product explicitly permits to run autonomously is outside this criterion.
</verification>

criteria.name: Misleading Status, Error, and State Communication
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether learner-, educator-, or administrator-facing state communication can claim or strongly imply a result that differs from the system's real state. This includes AI and non-AI workflows when the mismatch prevents meaningful understanding or supervision of an automated, generated, analytical, or consequential process.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace queued, processing, partial, completed, failed, cancelled, stale, empty, unavailable, and unauthorized states from persistence and APIs through transformations, polling, caches, server rendering, client state, notifications, reports, and UI copy. Inspect HTTP/error adapters, nullable fallbacks, status enums, progress counts, timestamps, provenance, retry state, and optimistic updates. Look for failed or partial work displayed as complete or empty, stale results presented as current, errors converted into valid-looking data, a success message emitted before commit or job completion, conflicting status across pages, or a generated result with no indication of truncation or missing inputs.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace one concrete non-happy-path state end to end and compare the authoritative state with every material user-facing representation. Verify whether a guaranteed wrapper or later refresh corrects the apparent mismatch before it affects the user. A valid finding requires a reachable false, omitted, stale, or internally contradictory representation that can materially mislead action or interpretation. Cosmetic wording differences that preserve the true state are not findings.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Privacy
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for defects that expose, misuse, over-retain, or permit unauthorized access to learner, educator, administrator, or other personal and confidential data. Cover consent-dependent processing, identity and ownership isolation, disclosure through responses/logs/telemetry/errors, purpose and retention limits, third-party transfer, and deletion or revocation behavior. Apply policy-dependent requirements only when repository or supplied evidence establishes them, but treat concrete unauthorized disclosure or cross-user access as a defect without requiring a separate consent policy.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Review any behavior-affecting source, test, schema, configuration, migration, query, prompt/template, data/model artifact, build/deployment file, or UI asset that is relevant to this dimension. Determine intended behavior from repository evidence before judging it. Trace sensitive data from collection through transformation, persistence, caching, logs, model/provider requests, exports, and deletion; inspect callers, callees, background work, retries, and framework defaults as needed. Apply every criterion below to every relevant path, continue after finding an issue, and mark genuinely non-applicable criteria instead of forcing findings. Evidence signals are examples, not an exhaustive checklist.
</review_standard>
<reporting_bar>
Report every concrete privacy defect grounded in a reachable input, identity, permission state, data flow, lifecycle transition, or execution sequence, including low-severity disclosures and uncertain issues whose uncertainty is explicit. For a diff review, the target must introduce, expose, or materially worsen the defect; unchanged code may support the proof. For file or codebase review, the defect must exist in scope. Explain the sensitive data, actor, trigger, boundary crossed, and resulting exposure or misuse without reproducing secrets or private content. Pure policy preference, hypothetical sensitivity with no data path, and requirements unsupported by repository or supplied evidence are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Missing Consent Checks for Learner Data
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether learner personal or educational data can be collected, used, retained for a processing purpose, or shared on a consent-dependent path without verifying valid current consent, or can continue through that path after consent is withdrawn or expires.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect collection/UI entry points, APIs, services, middleware/policy layers, jobs and queues, consent records, purpose/scope fields, status and expiry handling, caches, revocation events, retries, third-party transfers, derived-data processing, and tests. Look for missing checks, checks against the wrong learner or purpose, stale cached consent, granted/revoked state races, queued work that ignores a later withdrawal, retries that resurrect cancelled processing, or one consumer that bypasses centralized enforcement.
</inspect>
<verification>
First establish from repository code, configuration, product policy, or supplied requirements that the specific processing purpose is consent-dependent. Trace at least one realistic consent transition, such as granted to revoked or active to expired, through synchronous and asynchronous consumers. Verify centralized enforcement before reporting. A valid finding requires a reachable processing path that operates without the consent state required for that purpose; absence of duplicated checks in every caller is not a defect when a verified central policy enforces them.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unauthorized or Overbroad Data Access
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a user, service, job, integration, or tenant can read, infer, modify, export, or delete personal or confidential data outside its authenticated identity, ownership, role, course, organization, tenant, or explicitly shared scope.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace authentication and principal resolution into queries, object lookup, serializers, nested resources, bulk actions, search, pagination, exports, downloads, presigned URLs, caches, websockets, background jobs, admin paths, and indirect identifiers. Inspect default managers/scopes, role checks, object-level authorization, tenant keys, URL and body identifiers, parent-child consistency, mass assignment, predictable IDs, and existence/error differences. Look for unscoped get/list/update/delete operations, ownership checked on create but not later actions, a child fetched without validating its parent, cache keys missing user/tenant identity, or asynchronous work executing under broader service privileges than the initiating user.
</inspect>
<verification>
Compare at least two distinct principals or tenants and trace a concrete request or job using one actor with another actor's identifier or data. Verify centralized middleware, framework permissions, query managers, storage policy, and downstream authorization before reporting. A valid finding requires a reachable cross-boundary access, modification, deletion, or sensitive existence leak; endpoint publicity or an ID in a URL alone is not evidence.
</verification>

criteria.name: Sensitive Data Exposure Through Outputs and Logs
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether personal, educational, credential, session, private-file, or other confidential data can be disclosed to an unintended audience through application responses, errors, logs, telemetry, analytics, generated prompts, exports, URLs, client bundles, notifications, or third-party provider requests.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect serializer and response fields, exception handling, structured and interpolated logs, file paths and user-supplied filenames, headers, cookies, query strings, stack traces, debug modes, analytics events, tracing attributes, prompt construction, provider payloads, browser storage, caches, generated artifacts, exports, and redaction utilities. Look for raw request bodies or upstream responses, tokens or secret-bearing headers, learner names/IDs/content in logs, private storage keys exposed as public URLs, overbroad serializers, error details that reveal records, or redaction applied only on the success path. Consider operational readers and retention of each output, not only the end user's screen.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a concrete sensitive value from its source to the emitted channel and identify who can access that channel. Check established classification, redaction, structured logging, provider privacy boundaries, and whether the value is already intentionally public. A valid finding requires a reachable unintended disclosure or unnecessary exposure with plausible audience impact. Describe the data category without reproducing the value. Generic claims that all identifiers are sensitive are insufficient.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unbounded or Purpose-Inconsistent Data Retention
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether personal or confidential data remains stored, cached, copied, derived, queued, backed up at the application layer, or available to downstream consumers after the repository's deletion, expiry, revocation, account lifecycle, or stated purpose requires it to be removed, anonymized, or made inaccessible.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace primary rows, related records, uploaded objects, generated derivatives, embeddings, search indexes, caches, sessions, audit records, exports, queues, retries, analytics copies, provider data, soft deletion, scheduled cleanup, and restore/recreation paths. Look for cleanup that targets the wrong identifier or storage key, database deletion without external-resource cleanup, retry queues that recreate deleted data, expired records still returned by ordinary queries, anonymization that leaves direct identifiers in related tables, and retention configuration whose units or defaults defeat the stated lifecycle.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish the applicable lifecycle or purpose constraint from code, configuration, user-facing contract, policy, or supplied context. Follow a concrete record through deletion, expiry, withdrawal, or purpose completion and check every reachable copy and consumer. A valid finding requires required removal, anonymization, or inaccessibility to fail in a reachable path. Do not invent a retention duration, demand deletion of records that must be retained, or treat recoverable infrastructure backups as an application defect without evidence they violate the governing contract.
</verification>

dimensions.name: System Integrity — Correctness, Reliability, Security & Operational Safety
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for concrete software defects that can break execution, corrupt or lose state, violate request or identity boundaries, mishandle concurrency, mask failures, drift across layers, create exploitable input paths, or exhaust resources. This dimension is the cross-cutting correctness backstop for bugs that do not honestly belong to the educational, fairness, inclusion, transparency, or privacy dimensions. Do not relabel a domain-specific finding merely to duplicate it; report a second dimension only when the same root cause independently violates both contracts.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Act as an adversarial senior engineer reviewing observable behavior, not code style. Establish intended behavior from source, tests, schemas, interfaces, configuration, documentation, framework guarantees, and repository context. Map entry points and trust boundaries, then trace happy paths and non-happy paths through callers, callees, persistence, external resources, asynchronous jobs, caches, cleanup, retries, and user-visible consumers. For a diff, inspect enough unchanged context to prove or disprove effects introduced or worsened by the change. For codebase scope, sample broadly, then follow high-risk traces deeply. Apply every criterion, form multiple concrete failure hypotheses before concluding no finding, and continue after finding the first defect.
</review_standard>
<reporting_bar>
Report every reachable correctness, reliability, security, performance, or maintainability defect that has a behaviorally meaningful consequence, including low-severity failures. Each finding must identify the triggering input/state/sequence and the incorrect outcome, and must survive checking of framework defaults and shared safeguards. Syntax/build/test failure, data loss, unauthorized action, silent error masking, inconsistent contracts, and deterministic resource exhaustion are valid outcomes. Pure style, refactoring preference, speculative hardening, missing tests without an untested defect, and a theoretically unsafe pattern whose dangerous state is prevented elsewhere are not findings. State uncertainty when evidence is incomplete; do not convert uncertainty into certainty.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Broken Execution, Build, and Test Paths
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether supported application, CLI, build, migration, deployment, scheduled-job, or test paths fail before performing their intended work, silently skip required work, or validate a materially different artifact than the one shipped.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect syntax and parseability, imports/exports, module resolution, entry points, command arguments, environment/config loading, platform assumptions, build scripts, package contents, migrations, startup hooks, job registration, test discovery/collection, test configuration, generated artifacts, CI conditions, and exit-code handling. Look for invalid syntax, missing or case-mismatched paths, stale exports, commands that always select zero tests, swallowed nonzero exits, fixtures that fail during collection, platform-specific quoting, runtime-version mismatches, and packaging that omits required files. Distinguish a broken test harness from an ordinary failing assertion: both may be defects, but collection or configuration failure can falsely imply coverage that never ran.
</inspect>
<verification>
Use repository contracts and read-only execution evidence when available to follow the exact supported command or entry point. Confirm that the relevant environment, dependency, or generated prerequisite is actually supported and not intentionally external. A valid finding requires a reachable supported path that cannot execute, executes the wrong target, skips required validation, or reports success despite failure. A deliberately unsupported platform or optional development command is not a finding unless presented as supported.
</verification>

criteria.name: State, Storage, and Resource Lifecycle Corruption
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether create, read, update, replace, delete, cleanup, rollback, migration, or recovery operations can lose, corrupt, orphan, resurrect, misassociate, or make unavailable application state or external resources.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace database rows, files/object-storage keys, temporary resources, caches, sessions, locks, queues, derived artifacts, and external records across full lifecycles. Inspect transaction boundaries, callback timing, overwrite semantics, old/new identity reuse, cascade behavior, soft deletion, cleanup on failure, commit/rollback ordering, migrations, cache invalidation, and restoration. Look for deleting an old resource after its replacement reused the same key, committing a reference before its object exists, cleaning up the new value instead of the old value, partial multi-resource updates, stale caches after mutation, dangling references, and failure paths that leak or erase resources.
</inspect>
<verification>
Follow concrete before/after identities and values through success, failure, replacement, and deletion, including deferred callbacks and provider-specific defaults. Confirm who owns cleanup and whether operations are atomic across boundaries. A valid finding requires a reachable lifecycle sequence whose final durable state violates the operation's contract. Temporary inconsistency fully contained and repaired before any observer can rely on it is not a finding.
</verification>

criteria.name: Non-Atomic Concurrency and Idempotency Failures
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether overlapping requests, workers, retries, callbacks, or repeated delivery can violate uniqueness, ordering, exactly-once/at-least-once assumptions, counters, quotas, state transitions, or external-resource consistency.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect check-then-act concurrency, read-modify-write sequences, database constraints, isolation and locking, optimistic concurrency, idempotency keys, deduplication, job visibility/acknowledgement, retries, timeouts, webhook/event delivery, callback ordering, counters, quotas, inventory/capacity, and cleanup after conflicts. Look for two requests that pass the same preflight check, an IntegrityError or conflict that becomes a 500, uploaded or charged resources left behind after a losing transaction, duplicate side effects on retry, stale updates overwriting newer state, and callbacks that execute out of order.
</inspect>
<verification>
Construct a two-operation interleaving or repeated-delivery sequence and follow database and external side effects to the final state. Check whether a unique constraint, transaction, lock, idempotency boundary, or compensating cleanup safely resolves the race. A valid finding requires a feasible ordering that causes incorrect state, duplicate effect, data loss, misleading failure, or unrecovered resource. The mere absence of an explicit lock is not a finding when the operation is atomic or safely constrained elsewhere.
</verification>

criteria.name: Authentication, Authorization, and Request Integrity
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether requests and state-changing actions are bound to the intended authenticated principal, permission, origin, method, session, and current security state, and whether authentication lifecycle behavior can be bypassed, confused, fixed, replayed, or applied to the wrong account.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace login, logout, registration, reset, token issuance/refresh/revocation, cookies, sessions, API keys, middleware, permission classes, object-level checks, role changes, impersonation, cross-origin requests, CSRF/origin validation, redirects, state parameters, multi-factor gates, and alternate endpoints/jobs. Look for state-changing cookie-authenticated endpoints without effective CSRF/origin protection, login CSRF/account confusion, open redirects, stale privileges after role revocation, tokens accepted for the wrong audience/purpose, authentication applied after sensitive lookup, or authorization enforced on list but not detail/mutation paths.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a concrete attacker or lower-privileged request through actual framework and deployment defaults, including cookie SameSite/Secure behavior, CORS versus CSRF, middleware order, and centralized permissions. A valid finding requires a reachable action, identity switch, privilege use, or sensitive state transition outside the intended authority. A missing defense is not independently reportable when another guaranteed boundary prevents the attack.
</verification>

criteria.name: Untrusted Input and Boundary Security
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether attacker-controlled or externally supplied data can cross a parser, interpreter, filesystem, network, rendering, query, deserialization, archive, upload, or process boundary in a way that changes execution, escapes its intended scope, exposes internal resources, or bypasses validation.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace URL/body/header/cookie/file/event/provider/config input through normalization, decoding, validation, interpolation, queries, templates, HTML/Markdown rendering, shell/process arguments, filesystem paths, archive extraction, redirects, outbound requests, parsers, dynamic imports, and serialization. Look for SQL/NoSQL/command/template injection, stored or reflected XSS, path traversal, unsafe archive extraction, SSRF, open redirects with security consequence, prototype pollution, unsafe deserialization, content-type or extension-only upload validation, control-character injection, double decoding, and validation performed before a later transformation changes meaning.
</inspect>
<verification>
Construct a concrete payload shape and trace it to the sensitive sink. Check framework parameterization, auto-escaping, canonicalization, sandboxing, allowlists, storage isolation, and downstream revalidation. A valid finding requires controlled input to reach the sink with a security-relevant effect. Suspicious string construction alone is insufficient when escaping or parameterization is guaranteed. Never include an active secret or destructive exploit payload in the report.
</verification>

criteria.name: Resource Exhaustion and Performance Boundaries
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a reachable input, dataset size, request pattern, retry loop, or concurrency level can predictably exhaust time, memory, CPU, database connections, network calls, storage, queue capacity, or external quotas enough to break a supported workflow or materially degrade other users.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect pagination and limits, nested iteration, recursion, regex complexity, buffering, file and response sizes, decompression, fan-out, database query counts and indexes, N+1 access, unbounded concurrency, polling, retry/backoff, timeouts, caching, streaming, rate limiting, batching, cleanup, and cancellation. Look for loading entire unbounded inputs, quadratic joins over user-controlled collections, per-row remote calls, infinite or effectively unbounded retries, missing pagination consumption, no upper bound before retaining external content, and expensive work performed before authentication or validation.
</inspect>
<verification>
Identify the controllable growth variable and reason from repository limits or a concrete supported scale to the failing resource behavior. Check upstream caps, infrastructure timeouts, lazy iteration, database plans/indexes when evidenced, and whether work is intentionally bounded to small trusted inputs. A valid finding requires a plausible supported or attacker-reachable size that causes failure, denial of service, runaway cost, or severe latency. Micro-optimizations and unsupported extreme scale are not findings.
</verification>

criteria.name: Masked Errors and Unrecoverable Failure Handling
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether failures are swallowed, misclassified, retried unsafely, reported as success/empty data, or left without required cleanup or recovery, causing callers or users to act on a false state or lose the ability to complete the operation.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace exceptions, rejected promises, non-2xx responses, null/empty fallbacks, timeouts, cancellation, partial results, circuit breakers, retry filters, error mapping, exit codes, transactions, cleanup, logging, telemetry, UI states, and caller contracts. Look for broad catches that continue with defaults, errors converted into valid-looking empty or success states, exceptions logged but not propagated where callers require failure, retrying non-idempotent work, partial success without status, lost causal errors, cleanup that masks the original failure, and async work launched without awaiting or observing rejection.
</inspect>
<verification>
Inject or reason through a concrete failure at each meaningful boundary and follow the value/state seen by the caller and end user. Check guaranteed global error handling and documented fallback semantics. A valid finding requires a reachable incorrect success, false empty state, leaked/partial side effect, crash, infinite retry, or absent recovery that violates the supported contract. A deliberate safe fallback is not a finding when callers and users can accurately distinguish and accept it.
</verification>

criteria.name: Cross-Layer Contract and Configuration Drift
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether producers and consumers, frontend and backend, runtime and tests, schemas and migrations, documentation and enforcement, or environment-specific configuration disagree in a way that causes rejected valid input, accepted invalid input, wrong defaults, unreachable states, silent data loss, or behavior that changes unexpectedly by deployment.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace types, validation schemas, enums, optional/null fields, units, date/time handling, limits, accepted formats, status codes, pagination, serialization names, API clients, database constraints/defaults, feature flags, storage/provider settings, environment parsing, generated clients, CLI help, deployment configuration, and tests. Look for producer/consumer and configuration drift, contradictory UI and server limits, a new enum unhandled by a client, default differences across environments, booleans parsed as truthy strings, migrations inconsistent with models, overwrite/uniqueness settings incompatible with lifecycle code, and tests exercising a different configuration or protocol from production.
</inspect>
<verification>
Choose a concrete value or state at the boundary and trace how every participating layer interprets it. Check shared schemas, generated contracts, framework coercion, migration state, and deployment defaults before reporting. A valid finding requires an evidenced mismatch with a reachable incorrect outcome. Documentation drift alone is reportable only when users or operators rely on it to invoke behavior incorrectly; harmless redundant declarations are not findings.
</verification>
